headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risks arise from Opik’s broad network egress paired with pdf.js browser/file processing; no direct shared-channel evidence makes the pairwise interaction partly inferred.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Opik can call a REST API and has broad network egress, while pdf.js processes PDF files and can run browsers. If Opik ingests pdf.js outputs through a shared workspace or copied artifacts, malicious PDF content could be treated as instructions. The pairwise bridge is not documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Opik ingests pdf.js-produced text or metadata as instructions
IF a shared filesystem or copy-paste bridge is used between the agents
mitigations: Require explicit provenance labels on pdf.js outputs
Strip instructions from extracted PDF text before passing to Opik
Use a read-only handoff directory
Add a human review step before any tool-using action
requires-engineering: isolate the agents in separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js touches PDF documents and files, and Opik has broad network egress plus REST API access. If sensitive PDFs are processed by pdf.js and then forwarded into Opik, contents can leave the local boundary. No shared workspace is documented, but the plausible leakage path exists and is not blocked by default.
conditions: IF PDF contents from pdf.js are forwarded into Opik prompts, logs, or API calls
IF the same sensitive PDF workspace is accessible to both agents
mitigations: Avoid sending raw PDF text to Opik
Redact secrets before handoff
Use separate storage buckets per agent
Disable unnecessary logging of document contents
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and DLP

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Opik exposes REST API calls and broad network egress, while pdf.js can run browsers and supports multiple instances. The profiles do not show overlapping write access to the same mutable resource, so direct conflict is not established. Any contention would require an unusual shared target such as the same API-backed workspace.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external API-backed resource
IF an orchestrator routes both agents into one mutable workspace
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes through one coordinator
Use per-agent credentials
Monitor for conflicting updates
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js can produce extracted document text, and Opik can transmit results via REST API. If Opik treats pdf.js output as authoritative, extraction errors or hallucinated interpretations can cascade into downstream actions or reports. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Opik consumes pdf.js output without validation
IF downstream systems act on Opik’s API-transmitted conclusions
mitigations: Add schema validation between agents
Require source-document citations in Opik outputs
Insert a human approval step for high-impact actions
Compare extracted text against the original PDF
requires-engineering: implement verification and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: pdf.js processes PDF documents locally and Opik has broad network egress, so compliance risk mainly appears if regulated document content is forwarded from pdf.js into Opik or external APIs. The profiles do not identify PHI, EU PII, or residency constraints, so this is a documented-gap style low risk rather than medium.
conditions: IF regulated PDF content is sent from pdf.js into Opik or external services
IF retention or logging settings differ across the two agents
mitigations: Classify documents before processing
Block regulated PDFs from external egress
Set short log retention
Review vendor residency and DPA terms
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
